```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

```{r model-meta, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
mod <- readModelDb("Hunt_2024_renal_transporter_ontogeny")
ui <- rxode2::rxode(mod)
cat("* Citation: ", ui$reference, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Description: ", ui$description, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.13102>\n")
```

Hunt 2024 estimates how the activity of ten renal transporters matures from
preterm birth to adulthood, for use in pediatric physiologically-based
pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models. Transporter expression measured in post-mortem
kidney cortex was normalised to the mean mature level, and a Hill function of
postmenstrual age (PMA) was fitted by maximum likelihood with a lognormal,
heteroscedastic error. The result is, for every age, a lognormal distribution of
the ontogeny scaling factor (OSF): the fraction of mature transporter activity
that multiplies the adult transporter concentration in a PBPK kidney.

The paper then applies the OAT3, MATE1 and P-gp profiles in PK-Sim v11 pediatric
PBPK models of acyclovir, ciprofloxacin, furosemide and meropenem. Those drug
models are built on the PK-Sim whole-body platform: their organ volumes, blood
flows and partition coefficients come from the platform database rather than
from the paper, so they are not reproduced here. This model is the ontogeny
layer only, the part of the paper that is fully specified by its own equations
and tables.

# Population

The ontogeny data are the renal transporter expression measurements of Cheung
2019 (doi:10.1002/cpt.1516) from post-mortem renal cortical tissue obtained from
biobanks in the United States and the Netherlands. Protein abundance was used
where available; preterm neonates had only mRNA data, which were normalised to
mature mRNA in the same way and pooled with the protein data. Mature expression
was the mean over donors older than 5.5 years PMA (288 weeks; n = 23 per
transporter), after a Welch t-test found no difference between donors aged
5.5-18 years and those over 18 years. Each profile rests on 61 to 71 data points
spanning 25 weeks PMA to over 30 years (Supplementary Table S1). MRP2 and MRP4
had no protein data and were fitted to mRNA alone; URAT1 and BCRP had no preterm
neonate data. Sex, race and body size were not reported.

```{r population}
str(mod()$population)
```

# Source trace

Every value is in `inst/modeldb/endogenous/Hunt_2024_renal_transporter_ontogeny.R`
with its source in a trailing comment. The parameters are the first (lognormal,
combined protein and mRNA) block of a / b / s rows in Supplementary Table S1.

| Equation / parameter | Value | Source location |
|----------------------|-------|-----------------|
| Median OSF | `f = [1 + (a / PMA)^b]^-1`, PMA in years | Equation 1 |
| Lognormal likelihood | `ln(y / f) ~ N(0, sigma^2)` | Equation 2 |
| Log-scale SD | `sigma = s * exp(-f)` | Equation 3 |
| Use in PBPK | `[RT]ped = [RT]adult * OSF(PMA)` | Equation 4 |
| `oat3_t50`, `oat3_hill`, `oat3_sd0` | 1.081, 5.948, 1.279 | Table S1, OAT3 |
| `oat1_t50`, `oat1_hill`, `oat1_sd0` | 1.000, 7.602, 1.31 | Table S1, OAT1 |
| `pgp_t50`, `pgp_hill`, `pgp_sd0` | 1.001, 4.565, 1.066 | Table S1, P-gp |
| `mate1_t50`, `mate1_hill`, `mate1_sd0` | 0.824, 5.488, 1.116 | Table S1, MATE1 |
| `mate2k_t50`, `mate2k_hill`, `mate2k_sd0` | 0.661, 8.221, 1.256 | Table S1, MATE2 |
| `bcrp_t50`, `bcrp_hill`, `bcrp_sd0` | 0.7, 2.7, 1.1 (manual) | Table S1, BCRP |
| `mrp2_t50`, `mrp2_hill`, `mrp2_sd0` | 1.0, 3.9, 1.7 (manual) | Table S1, MRP2 |
| `mrp4_t50`, `mrp4_hill`, `mrp4_sd0` | 0.6, 5.0, 1.3 (manual) | Table S1, MRP4 |
| `urat1_t50`, `urat1_hill`, `urat1_sd0` | 0.982, 8.732, 1.294 | Table S1, URAT1 |
| `oct2_t50`, `oct2_hill`, `oct2_sd0` | 0.902, 8.670, 1.496 | Table S1, OCT2 |
| `etalont_<transporter>` | standard normal, variance 1 | Equations 2-3; Methods, OSF sampled per virtual individual |

Table S1 marks the BCRP, MRP2 and MRP4 lognormal values as set by manual,
iterative adjustment against the visual fit and the likelihood, not by a
converged optimisation.

# Checks against the paper

```{r helpers}
mod0 <- rxode2::zeroRe(mod)
rt <- c("oat3", "oat1", "pgp", "mate1", "mate2k", "bcrp", "mrp2", "mrp4", "urat1", "oct2")
rt_label <- c(
  oat3 = "OAT3", oat1 = "OAT1", pgp = "P-gp", mate1 = "MATE1",
  mate2k = "MATE-2K", bcrp = "BCRP", mrp2 = "MRP2", mrp4 = "MRP4",
  urat1 = "URAT1", oct2 = "OCT2"
)
solve_pma <- function(m, pma, ...) {
  d <- data.frame(id = seq_along(pma), time = 0, evid = 0, PAGE = pma)
  as.data.frame(rxode2::rxSolve(m, d, returnType = "data.frame", ...))
}
```

## Tabulated profiles (Supplementary Tables S2-S11)

Tables S2-S11 tabulate each lognormal profile as the median OSF and the
geometric standard deviation (GeoSD) by PMA. They are the form the paper
provides "for incorporation into PBPK models", so reproducing them is a
known-answer check on Equations 1 and 3 and on every transcribed parameter.
Nine PMA rows are compared for all ten transporters.

```{r tables-s2-s11}
pma_rows <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0)
tab_osf <- tibble::tribble(
  ~rt, ~table, ~p0.1, ~p0.5, ~p0.8, ~p1.0, ~p1.2, ~p1.5, ~p2.0, ~p3.0, ~p5.0,
  "oat3", "S2", 0.000, 0.010, 0.143, 0.387, 0.651, 0.875, 0.975, 0.998, 1.000,
  "oat1", "S3", 0.000, 0.005, 0.155, 0.500, 0.800, 0.956, 0.995, 1.000, 1.000,
  "pgp", "S4", 0.000, 0.040, 0.264, 0.499, 0.696, 0.864, 0.959, 0.993, 0.999,
  "mate1", "S5", 0.000, 0.061, 0.459, 0.743, 0.887, 0.964, 0.992, 0.999, 1.000,
  "mate2k", "S6", 0.000, 0.091, 0.827, 0.968, 0.993, 0.999, 1.000, 1.000, 1.000,
  "bcrp", "S7", 0.005, 0.287, 0.589, 0.724, 0.811, 0.887, 0.945, 0.981, 0.995,
  "mrp2", "S8", 0.000, 0.063, 0.295, 0.500, 0.671, 0.829, 0.937, 0.986, 0.998,
  "mrp4", "S9", 0.000, 0.287, 0.808, 0.928, 0.970, 0.990, 0.998, 1.000, 1.000,
  "urat1", "S10", 0.000, 0.003, 0.143, 0.539, 0.852, 0.976, 0.998, 1.000, 1.000,
  "oct2", "S11", 0.000, 0.006, 0.260, 0.709, 0.922, 0.988, 0.999, 1.000, 1.000
)
tab_gsd <- tibble::tribble(
  ~rt, ~p0.1, ~p0.5, ~p0.8, ~p1.0, ~p1.2, ~p1.5, ~p2.0, ~p3.0, ~p5.0,
  "oat3", 3.591, 3.546, 3.028, 2.384, 1.948, 1.704, 1.620, 1.602, 1.601,
  "oat1", 3.706, 3.681, 3.071, 2.213, 1.801, 1.655, 1.623, 1.619, 1.619,
  "pgp", 2.903, 2.783, 2.267, 1.910, 1.702, 1.567, 1.504, 1.484, 1.480,
  "mate1", 3.051, 2.858, 2.023, 1.700, 1.583, 1.530, 1.512, 1.508, 1.507,
  "mate2k", 3.512, 3.148, 1.732, 1.612, 1.593, 1.588, 1.588, 1.588, 1.588,
  "bcrp", 2.987, 2.283, 1.841, 1.705, 1.631, 1.573, 1.534, 1.511, 1.502,
  "mrp2", 5.473, 4.936, 3.545, 2.804, 2.385, 2.100, 1.946, 1.885, 1.871,
  "mrp4", 3.706, 2.834, 1.986, 1.866, 1.828, 1.810, 1.804, 1.802, 1.802,
  "urat1", 3.648, 3.638, 3.172, 2.318, 1.925, 1.809, 1.790, 1.789, 1.789,
  "oct2", 4.466, 4.434, 3.371, 2.336, 2.045, 1.972, 1.960, 1.959, 1.959
)
to_long <- function(tab, value) {
  tab |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("p"), names_to = "pma", values_to = value) |>
    dplyr::mutate(pma = as.numeric(sub("^p", "", pma)))
}
paper <- to_long(dplyr::select(tab_osf, -table), "osf_paper") |>
  dplyr::left_join(to_long(tab_gsd, "gsd_paper"), by = c("rt", "pma"))

sim <- solve_pma(mod0, pma_rows)
model_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(rt, function(r) {
  data.frame(
    rt = r, pma = sim$PAGE,
    osf_model = sim[[paste0("ont_", r, "_med")]],
    gsd_model = sim[[paste0("gsd_", r)]]
  )
}))
cmp <- dplyr::left_join(paper, model_long, by = c("rt", "pma")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    osf_diff = osf_model - osf_paper,
    gsd_diff = gsd_model - gsd_paper
  )

# Median OSF: every row of every table within the 3-decimal rounding of the
# printed values (Table S1 itself is rounded, so allow two units in the last
# printed place).
stopifnot(max(abs(cmp$osf_diff)) < 0.002)

cmp |>
  dplyr::group_by(rt) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    max_abs_osf_diff = max(abs(osf_diff)),
    max_abs_gsd_diff = max(abs(gsd_diff)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rt = rt_label[rt]) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Transporter" = rt,
    "Max abs. difference, median OSF" = max_abs_osf_diff,
    "Max abs. difference, GeoSD" = max_abs_gsd_diff
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

The median OSF reproduces every tabulated row for all ten transporters. The
GeoSD reproduces Tables S2-S8 (OAT3, OAT1, P-gp, MATE1, MATE-2K, BCRP, MRP2) to
the third decimal. For MRP4, URAT1 and OCT2 (Tables S9-S11) the tabulated GeoSD
is wider at maturity than Equation 3 gives; this is examined in "Assumptions and
deviations" below.

```{r gsd-eq3-check}
eq3_ok <- cmp |> dplyr::filter(!rt %in% c("mrp4", "urat1", "oct2"))
stopifnot(max(abs(eq3_ok$gsd_diff)) < 0.004)
```

## Median ontogeny profiles (Figure 2a)

```{r fig2a, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 2a of Hunt 2024: median ontogeny scaling factor of each renal transporter against PMA. The Hayton reference curve of the published figure is not part of this model."}
pma_grid <- seq(0.05, 2.5, by = 0.01)
curves <- solve_pma(mod0, pma_grid)
curves_long <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(rt, function(r) {
  data.frame(rt = rt_label[[r]], pma = curves$PAGE, osf = curves[[paste0("ont_", r, "_med")]])
}))
ggplot(curves_long, aes(pma, osf, colour = rt, linetype = rt)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "PMA (years)", y = "Median ontogeny scaling factor", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

## P-gp distribution (Figure 2b)

Figure 2b draws the P-gp median with dashed lines two standard deviations away,
which on the lognormal scale is `median * GeoSD^2` and `median / GeoSD^2`. The
published mature band runs from about 0.45 to 2.2.

```{r fig2b, fig.cap = "Replicates the curves of Figure 2b of Hunt 2024: P-gp median OSF with the two-standard-deviation band. The observed data and the PK-Sim virtual population of the published panel are not reproduced."}
pgp <- solve_pma(mod0, seq(0.05, 3.5, by = 0.01)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lower = ont_pgp_med / gsd_pgp^2, upper = ont_pgp_med * gsd_pgp^2)
mature_pgp <- pgp[nrow(pgp), ]
c(lower = mature_pgp$lower, upper = mature_pgp$upper)
stopifnot(
  abs(mature_pgp$upper - 2.2) < 0.1,
  abs(mature_pgp$lower - 0.45) < 0.05
)
ggplot(pgp, aes(PAGE)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ont_pgp_med)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lower), linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = upper), linetype = "dashed", colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "PMA (years)", y = "P-gp ontogeny scaling factor") +
  theme_bw()
```

## OAT3 distributions by age (Figure 2c) from a virtual population

A stochastic solve draws one standard-normal deviate per subject and
transporter, so each virtual subject carries an OSF sampled from the
distribution for its age, as PK-Sim does for a population simulation. The
six ages are those of Figure 2c.

```{r fig2c, fig.cap = "Replicates Figure 2c of Hunt 2024: distribution of the OAT3 ontogeny scaling factor at six pediatric ages, from 200 virtual subjects per age."}
ages <- c(
  "Preterm (31 wk)" = 31, "Newborn (42 wk)" = 42, "2 months (47 wk)" = 47,
  "4 months (57 wk)" = 57, "6 months (63 wk)" = 63, "3 years (198 wk)" = 198
)
# Weeks to years at the paper's own conversion (938 weeks = 18 years).
wk_per_yr <- 938 / 18
rxode2::rxSetSeed(2024)
vp <- solve_pma(mod, rep(ages / wk_per_yr, each = 200))
vp$age <- factor(rep(names(ages), each = 200), levels = names(ages))
ggplot(vp, aes(ont_oat3, colour = age)) +
  geom_density(bounds = c(0, Inf)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "OAT3 ontogeny scaling factor", y = "Probability density", colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

The sampled distributions are checked against the model's own median and
geometric SD at each age. The comparison is on the median and on the
interquartile spread, which are robust to which subjects land in the tails.

```{r fig2c-check}
vp_chk <- vp |>
  dplyr::group_by(age) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    median_sampled = median(ont_oat3),
    median_model = dplyr::first(ont_oat3_med),
    log_iqr_sampled = diff(quantile(log(ont_oat3), c(0.25, 0.75))),
    log_iqr_model = 2 * qnorm(0.75) * log(dplyr::first(gsd_oat3)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
vp_chk |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Age" = age,
    "Median, sampled" = median_sampled,
    "Median, Equation 1" = median_model,
    "Log IQR, sampled" = log_iqr_sampled,
    "Log IQR, Equation 3" = log_iqr_model
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
stopifnot(
  # 200 draws: the sampled median sits within ~0.2 log units of the true one.
  all(abs(log(vp_chk$median_sampled / vp_chk$median_model)) < 0.4),
  all(abs(vp_chk$log_iqr_sampled / vp_chk$log_iqr_model - 1) < 0.3)
)
```

## Mature OAT3 variability (Discussion)

The Discussion reports that sampling the mature OAT3 distribution gives a
coefficient of variation of 0.50, against 0.44 and 0.48 measured in adult
tissue. For a lognormal, CV = sqrt(exp(sigma^2) - 1).

```{r oat3-cv}
mature <- solve_pma(mod0, 30)
cv_oat3 <- sqrt(exp(log(mature$gsd_oat3)^2) - 1)
cv_oat3
stopifnot(abs(cv_oat3 - 0.50) < 0.005)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **Only the final lognormal profiles are encoded.** Supplementary Table S1 also
  gives normally distributed profiles (Equations S1-S2, `sigma = s * f`) and
  lognormal profiles fitted to protein data alone, excluding the preterm mRNA
  data. The paper presents both as sensitivity analyses; its PBPK models and
  Tables S2-S11 use the lognormal, combined-data profiles, which are the ones
  encoded here. The alternative parameter sets are listed below for reference.

```{r alt-profiles}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Transporter, ~a_normal, ~b_normal, ~s_normal, ~a_protein, ~b_protein, ~s_protein,
  "OAT3", 1.072, 3.818, 0.399, 1.157, 1.752, 0.835,
  "OAT1", 1.062, 1.383, 0.456, 0.786, 1.914, 1.310,
  "P-gp", 0.860, 3.967, 0.394, 0.936, 3.044, 0.920,
  "MATE1", 0.8, 6, 0.35, 0.593, 2.080, 0.972,
  "MATE-2K", 0.65, 7.5, 0.4, 0.167, 13.523, 1.244,
  "BCRP", 0.001, 0.305, 0.301, 0.7, 2.7, 1.1,
  "MRP2", 0.9, 5.5, 0.47, NA, NA, NA,
  "MRP4", 0.6, 5.0, 0.45, NA, NA, NA,
  "URAT1", 0.884, 7.597, 0.470, 0.982, 8.732, 1.294,
  "OCT2", 0.827, 6.120, 0.451, 0.320, 0.619, 0.996
) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Normal: a (years)" = a_normal, "Normal: b" = b_normal, "Normal: s" = s_normal,
    "Protein only: a (years)" = a_protein, "Protein only: b" = b_protein,
    "Protein only: s" = s_protein
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Table S1, second (normal) and third (lognormal, protein only) blocks. MRP2 and MRP4 had no protein data.")
```

* **Equation 3 versus Tables S9-S11 (MRP4, URAT1, OCT2).** For these three
  transporters the tabulated GeoSD at maturity (1.802, 1.789, 1.959) is wider
  than Equation 3 gives with the Table S1 `s` (1.61, 1.61, 1.73), while the
  GeoSD at PMA 0.1 equals `exp(s)` exactly. All three tables, at every PMA, are
  reproduced instead by `sigma = s * exp(-0.8 * f)`, and the two-standard-deviation
  bands of Supplementary Figure S3 for these transporters (mature upper bounds
  near 3.25, 3.2 and 3.85) agree with the tables rather than with Equation 3. The
  other seven transporters follow Equation 3 exactly. The paper does not explain
  the difference. The model follows the printed Equation 3 for all ten
  transporters; a user who needs the tabulated MRP4, URAT1 or OCT2 variability
  should use the 0.8 factor shown below. Neither MRP4, URAT1 nor OCT2 is used in
  the paper's drug PBPK models.

```{r eq3-alternative}
alt <- cmp |>
  dplyr::filter(rt %in% c("mrp4", "urat1", "oct2")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    tibble::tibble(rt = c("mrp4", "urat1", "oct2"), s = c(1.31, 1.294, 1.496)),
    by = "rt"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(gsd_alt = exp(s * exp(-0.8 * osf_model)))
alt |>
  dplyr::filter(pma %in% c(0.1, 1.0, 5.0)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rt = rt_label[rt]) |>
  dplyr::select(rt, pma, gsd_paper, gsd_model, gsd_alt) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Transporter" = rt, "PMA (years)" = pma, "GeoSD, table" = gsd_paper,
    "GeoSD, Equation 3" = gsd_model, "GeoSD, factor 0.8" = gsd_alt
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
# The 0.8 factor reproduces every compared row of Tables S9-S11.
stopifnot(max(abs(alt$gsd_alt - alt$gsd_paper)) < 0.004)
```

* **MRP4 `s`.** Table S1 prints `s` = 1.3 for MRP4 (a manually adjusted value);
  Table S9's GeoSD of 3.706 at PMA 0.1, where the median is zero, implies 1.31.
  The model uses the printed 1.3. The 0.8-factor check above uses 1.31.
* **PMA in years.** Equation 1 is written with PMA in years, so the model's
  `PAGE` covariate is in years, not the register's default of months. Where the
  vignette converts weeks to years (Figure 2c) it uses the paper's own pairing
  of 938 weeks with 18 years.
* **Independent transporters.** The paper does not report correlations between
  transporters, and PK-Sim samples each ontogeny factor separately, so the ten
  deviates are independent. Each subject keeps the same deviate at every age,
  i.e. a subject's rank within the distribution is constant as it matures; the
  paper's population simulations are cross-sectional and do not address this.
* **URAT1 non-monotonic maturation.** The Discussion notes that URAT1 expression
  may peak near 3 years PMA before falling to adult levels, which the monotonic
  Hill function cannot capture.
* **Drug PBPK models not reproduced.** The acyclovir, ciprofloxacin, furosemide
  and meropenem PK-Sim models (deposited as `.pksim5` project files in the
  paper's supplementary material) depend on PK-Sim database physiology and are
  not encoded.
